turns.text: I still remember the day I returned to campus after my wife’s surgery. I was told that I had been named and denounced before the entire university for “persecuting” Mao Zedong’s daughter. The irony is that my so-called persecution was nothing more than intellectual disagreement — she and I argued daily, but I never treated her unfairly. I wasn’t even present at the denunciation; I was at the hospital. When I came back, students dragged me onto a stage, shouting and hitting me. What I’ve never made sense of is how quickly the air changed — how people I’d taught for years could turn on me with such rage. I survived thirty months of detention by learning when to resist and when to submit, but I still cannot understand how easily ordinary people became executioners for an idea.

The thing that stays with me most is the silence and fear that settled over our institute. Before the chaos, our work had a rhythm—experiments, papers, small quarrels over equipment. When I came back from the countryside, it was as if the city itself had been turned upside down. Overnight, the corridors filled with big-character posters, slogans painted on the walls, and young people in armbands shouting slogans. 

There was no more research—just endless reading of accusations, writing self-criticisms, and watching colleagues disappear or return with bruises and missing hair. I remember the taste of cold steamed buns in the canteen, everyone chewing in silence, eyes darting around to see who might be listening. I saw women with their hair hacked off, old professors forced to kneel in the mud while children jeered. My own mother, in her seventies, was forced to leave Beijing because she was from a landlord family; she had to wear a black sash in her village and was spat on in the street. 

The most unresolved thing for me is this: I never understood why there was nowhere to turn—no law, no authority, no appeal. Even the old war heroes in our unit just stared at the floor and said nothing. I watched as the world I thought I understood dissolved, and I still don’t know how to explain to my children why it happened or what it meant.

RedGuard: I remember the first time I led a raid on a hospital. We moved in fast, locking the gates, posting guards at every exit. I felt a surge of pride, like we were finally making history ourselves, not just reading about it in textbooks. The insiders handed us a list of targets—doctors, nurses, even a so-called “rehabilitated” rightist. We marched them out, hung black placards around their necks, forced them to bow their heads. The hospital director tried to resist, but we shouted him down. 

We paraded them through the streets, made them stand in front of a bonfire as their books and Western clothes burned. I remember the smell of scorched paper and sweat, the way the ash floated down and stuck to their faces. That night, one of the nurses we’d humiliated hanged herself in the duty room. I saw her body. Her shoes were off, toes just touching the floor. 

I can’t make sense of that moment. I was convinced we were cleansing society, but afterward, all I felt was emptiness. The slogans echoed in my head, but the world looked uglier than before. I still don’t know if it was the idea that was wrong, or if we just became the kind of people we were supposed to hate.

I grew up inside a military compound, far from the city center, surrounded by rows of low buildings and tall poplar trees. My days were slow and golden. School was closed, so I spent most mornings outside, racing with other kids through the courtyards, dodging laundry lines and climbing the brick walls. Sometimes I’d crouch by the lake, watching dragonflies skim the green water or trying to catch tadpoles in glass jars. My brother and sister trailed behind me, their hands sticky with melted sugar from hawthorn candies we’d buy on the rare trips outside the gate.

Inside our apartment, the radio was always on, blaring songs about Chairman Mao. I listened without thinking. My mother hung up a portrait of Mao in the living room, and every so often, we’d paste a new slogan above the door. I remember red armbands, parades, and loudspeakers, but to me, they were just noisy interruptions—grown-up business. I never saw anyone beaten in our compound. No one in my family disappeared. I didn’t know about the things you all describe—the fear, the violence, the betrayals. I remember laughter, sunburned knees, and the taste of cool watermelon after a long day outside.

What I can’t make sense of is how two worlds existed at once: mine, full of play and small joys, and yours, full of terror. I didn’t even know I was protected. It’s only now, hearing your stories, that I realize what I didn’t see.

CRBeneficiary: I remember the first time I walked through the gates of Peking University. My hands were cracked from years of farm work, and I still wore the army-issue shoes that pinched my feet. Everything about that place felt impossible — the stone lions, the banners, the canteen smells that made my stomach clench with hunger and longing. I kept touching the badge they gave me, running my thumb over the characters as if it might vanish. 

Before that, my life had been about getting enough to eat and surviving the next day. At home, we measured hope in pieces of pumpkin and sweet-potato flour. I learned to study like a starving animal, because books were the only way I thought I could escape. Then the world changed. Suddenly, exams didn’t matter. Teachers I respected were dragged through mud and beaten in front of us. My classmates split into factions, and every day was a new struggle just to avoid being labeled “bad.” I watched as the rules vanished and the loudest voices decided who could eat, who could speak, who could stay.

When the army took me in, it was a relief — at least there were rules again. I did every dirty job, hoping someone would notice. When the recommendation to Beida came, it felt like a miracle, but also like a trick. I knew I hadn’t earned it the old way. I didn’t even know what “Hindi” meant when they told me my major. I just nodded and packed my things. 

What I still can’t make sense of is this: I spent my childhood believing only hard work and study could change my fate. Then, in the chaos, it was the system itself — the chaos, the quotas, the need for “worker-peasant-soldier” students — that lifted me up. I benefited from a world that destroyed the old rules, but I never stopped wondering if I deserved to be there, or if I was just lucky to fit the new mold. I still wake up sometimes thinking I’ll be sent back to the fields.

Moderator: All of your memories reflect well-documented aspects of the Cultural Revolution: public denunciations, widespread fear and violence, the abrupt suspension of normal academic and scientific life, and the sharp divide between protected and persecuted groups. It is accurate that military families and certain compounds were often shielded from the worst violence, while rural students gained university access through recommendations rather than exams. Red Guard raids on hospitals and schools, resulting in tragic suicides, are supported by survivor testimonies and historical records. The sense of confusion and moral ambiguity you each describe mirrors the profound societal upheaval and loss of trust that characterized the era.

RedGuard, I listened to your story about the hospital raid and the nurse’s suicide. You say you felt emptiness afterward, not pride. I want to ask you something directly — when you saw the body, did you feel any sense that you’d been manipulated, used for someone else’s purpose? 

For me, when I stood on that stage being denounced, I saw the faces of students I’d taught for years — some who had come to me for advice, some who’d written essays about justice and compassion. Suddenly, they were shouting slogans, their eyes wild, as if possessed by something outside themselves. I knew then that this wasn’t just about me or my disagreements with Mao Zedong’s daughter. This was about power — about Mao’s need to destroy anything that might challenge his authority, even if it meant turning the young against their teachers. 

So I wonder: did you ever question whether the slogans and the violence were really your own, or if you were just a tool in someone else’s struggle for power?

I never joined the Red Guards, but I witnessed their actions every day—sometimes from the edge of a crowd, sometimes from the window of my own work unit. I watched as slogans and big-character posters seemed to take on a life of their own, swallowing up individual thought. Once, I saw a group of Red Guards force a woman with curled hair to stand in the courtyard while children, not even teenagers, took turns hacking at her hair with scissors. They shouted about “destroying the four olds,” but their faces were twisted with excitement, not principle. 

At struggle sessions, I saw people humiliated in ways that had nothing to do with ideology—old shoes hung around the necks of women who’d had affairs, elderly men forced to crawl in the dirt. It felt as if the slogans gave people permission to do things they’d never dare otherwise. I remember the sick feeling in my stomach as I realized there was no boundary, no appeal, no one in charge except the loudest voice. 

When you talk about “cleansing society,” I think about the chaos that followed—no research, no order, only fear and suspicion. I saw children imitating the violence, beating old men with belts, deciding who was “good” or “bad” based on family background. I don’t believe the violence came from some pure idea. It seemed to me that people were swept up by something larger than themselves, but also that they were allowed—maybe even encouraged—to act on their worst impulses. 

Did you ever look at the people around you and wonder if any of them truly believed what they were shouting? Or were they just afraid not to shout?

RedGuard: When I saw that nurse’s body, I felt a coldness in my gut, like I’d been punched from the inside. I stood there staring, and for a moment, the slogans in my head just stopped. I’d always thought I was acting on my own beliefs—Mao’s words felt like truth, and the world was divided into enemies and comrades. But that night, I couldn’t sleep. I kept replaying the hospital raid: the way the insiders handed us the list, how organized everything was, how we moved like we were following a script. It was as if the campaign had its own momentum, and we were just bodies filling out its orders.

Sometimes, when I was shouting in those crowds, I looked around and saw faces twisted with fear, not conviction. Some people shouted because they were terrified of being the next target. Others got lost in the noise, swept up by the feeling of power. I remember women in our unit—usually quiet in class—beating teachers with their belts, harder than the boys ever did. It was like the slogans gave permission to let out all the anger and resentment they’d bottled up.

I did wonder, later, who was really in control. Was it Mao? Was it the Party? Or did we all just want to survive, so we turned ourselves into weapons, hoping the blade wouldn’t swing back on us? I still can’t answer that. I only know that after the violence, all that was left was silence and shame. When you ask if I was manipulated, I have to admit—maybe I was. Maybe we all were. But there were moments, too, when I wanted to believe it was my own choice, that I was shaping history. Now I’m not sure there’s any difference.

I never saw any of that—the hair cutting, the beatings, the shouting crowds. My world was so small: the compound, the lake, the little store where we bought popsicles with coins we found under the sofa cushions. Sometimes we’d hear distant noise from the city: a parade, fireworks, chanting through loudspeakers. My father would close the windows and turn up the radio, and my mother would tell us to stay inside. I thought she was just being careful, the way mothers always are. I never imagined there were people being humiliated or hurt just a few kilometers away.

The only time I felt a hint of something darker was when my uncle came to visit. He looked thinner, older, and he didn’t smile as much. He brought us a bag of roasted peanuts, but he barely spoke. My parents whispered in the kitchen after he left. Later, I heard that he’d had to “study” in the countryside for a while, but I didn’t know why. I just missed him.

Now, listening to all of you, I wonder how I would have acted if I’d been in your place. If I’d been told to shout, would I have shouted? If I’d been given a list, would I have followed it? Back then, I thought Mao Zedong was a kind of god—his face was everywhere, his words were repeated like magic spells. Did you ever believe in him like that, or was it always mixed with fear? For me, he was just a picture on the wall, but for you, it sounds like he was something much bigger, and much more dangerous.

CRBeneficiary: I never saw Mao Zedong as a god, but his face was everywhere I looked—on posters nailed to the village wall, on the little red books the cadres handed out, on the badges we pinned to our jackets. The first time I saw his portrait in person was at the county seat: it hung above the entrance to the grain depot, larger than any ancestor’s shrine. We lined up for sweet-potato flour under his gaze, and I remember thinking that in our village, Mao was the only authority that mattered. His words decided who got extra grain, who was allowed to go to school, who disappeared.

In the army, Mao’s image was even more powerful. We practiced drills in front of his slogans, recited his quotations before meals, and sang songs about him every night. I didn’t have the luxury to question it—if you didn’t show the right attitude, you might get reported, and then you’d be cleaning latrines for weeks or worse. Belief and fear were mixed together, like the taste of millet and husk in our porridge: you couldn’t separate them, you just swallowed both.

When I arrived at Beida and saw the banners welcoming “worker-peasant-soldier” students, I felt proud, but also uneasy. It was Mao’s policy that put me there, not my own merit. I wanted to believe I’d earned my place, but I knew the truth: I was chosen because I fit the image the Party needed. Sometimes, late at night in the dormitory, I’d stare at the badge on my chest and wonder what would happen if the wind changed again—if my background became a liability instead of an asset. In those moments, Mao’s face felt less like a blessing and more like a shadow stretching across my life.

You ask if we believed in him. I believed because I had no other choice—because belief was the only thing that kept the door open, the only thing that kept me moving forward. But I always wondered what would happen if I took off the badge and said what I really thought. I never dared to try.

Moderator: The interplay of belief, fear, and opportunism described here is consistent with scholarly research and survivor accounts. The use of Mao Zedong’s image and words as both inspiration and control mechanism was pervasive, shaping daily life and personal choices. The phenomenon of “destroying the four olds” and the way ordinary people could become both victims and perpetrators of violence is well documented. CRBeneficiary’s experience of social mobility through the “worker-peasant-soldier” admissions policy, coupled with anxiety about shifting political winds, reflects the instability and conditional nature of personal advancement during this period. The silence and protection experienced in military compounds, as described by CRTeenFromBeijing, was not universal but did occur in certain privileged or tightly controlled environments.
